title: Backpropagation
description: Computing the gradient of a network's loss with the chain rule: computational graphs, the backward recursion, a worked example, vanishing gradients and gradient checking.
overview: Training a neural network means minimizing a loss J(θ) over millions or billions of parameters by gradient descent, so we need ∇J, the derivative of the loss with respect to every weight. Differentiating each weight separately would cost one forward pass per parameter. Backpropagation computes all the derivatives together in a single backward pass that costs about as much as one forward pass.

Backpropagation is the chain rule of calculus organized to reuse work. This chapter derives it for the multilayer network, works a complete numerical example, and then looks at the trouble that long chains of derivatives cause.
objectives: Evaluate and differentiate a function expressed as a computational graph by a forward and a backward pass.
Derive the backpropagation equations for a fully connected network.
Compute all the gradients of a small network by hand and apply a gradient step.
Explain vanishing and exploding gradients, and the role of the activation function.
Verify gradients numerically with gradient checking.

sections.title: Computational graphs and the chain rule
body: The goal is to find, for every weight, how much the loss would change if that weight were nudged up by a tiny amount. That number is the weight's share of the blame for the error. A weight deep inside the network affects the loss only through a long chain: it changes one unit, which changes the next layer, and so on until the output. The chain rule says how to combine effects along a chain: multiply them. If nudging x by 1 changes q by 1, and nudging q by 1 changes f by −4, then nudging x by 1 changes f by 1 × (−4) = −4. Backpropagation does this multiplication for every weight, starting at the output and moving backward so that shared pieces are computed once instead of once per weight.

Write the computation as a **computational graph**: each node is one simple operation (add, multiply, apply an activation) and each edge carries a value. The chain rule says that the derivative of the output with respect to any node is the sum, over the nodes it feeds, of the derivative of the output with respect to that node times the local derivative of that node with respect to this one:

The factor ∂f/∂v arrives from above (the **upstream gradient**), and ∂v/∂u is the **local gradient** of a single operation, which is simple. Starting at the output with ∂f/∂f = 1 and working backward through the graph, each node multiplies its upstream gradient by its local gradients and passes the products to its inputs.

example.title: Forward and backward on a small graph
example.problem: Compute f = (x + y)z at x = −2, y = 5, z = −4, and the gradient with respect to x, y and z.
solution: Forward: q = x + y = 3, and f = qz = −12.

Backward from ∂f/∂f = 1. The multiply node has local gradients ∂f/∂q = z = −4 and ∂f/∂z = q = 3, so these are the gradients at q and z. The add node has local gradients 1 and 1, so ∂f/∂x = ∂f/∂q · 1 = −4 and ∂f/∂y = −4.
Check by hand: f = (x + y)z, so ∂f/∂x = z = −4 and ∂f/∂z = x + y = 3. ✓

body.key: Reverse-mode differentiation gives the derivative of one scalar output with respect to all inputs in one backward sweep, at a cost proportional to one evaluation. A loss is a scalar and the parameters are many, which is the case that favors reverse mode. See Automatic Differentiation in the Computer Science book for how software does this.

sections.title: The backpropagation equations
body: The idea in words: at the output, the error is how far the prediction is from the label. Each hidden unit then gets blamed in proportion to how strongly it was connected to the units that made errors (the weights, used in reverse), and only to the extent that it was able to affect them (the activation's slope). This blame is called the error signal, and each weight's gradient is its error signal times the input that weight was applied to: a big input and a big blame mean a big gradient.

Consider the L-layer network of the previous chapter, z^{[l]} = W^{[l]}a^{[l−1]} + b^{[l]} and a^{[l]} = g(z^{[l]}), with loss J on the output. Define the **error signal** of layer l as the gradient of the loss with respect to its pre-activation:
**Output layer.** For the standard pairings (sigmoid or softmax output with cross-entropy, identity output with squared error) the derivative collapses to the prediction error:
**Hidden layers.** The pre-activation z^{[l]} influences the loss only through z^{[l+1]} = W^{[l+1]} g(z^{[l]}) + b^{[l+1]}. The chain rule gives

where ⊙ is the elementwise (Hadamard) product. The transpose of the weight matrix carries the error from layer l + 1 back to the units in layer l that contributed to it, and g′ gates it by how sensitive each unit's output was.
For a batch, sum or average these over the examples. The algorithm is:

list: **Forward pass**: compute and store every z^{[l]} and a^{[l]}, then the loss.
**Backward pass**: compute δ^{[L]}, and then for l = L, …, 1 compute ∂J/∂W^{[l]} and ∂J/∂b^{[l]}, and δ^{[l−1]}.
**Update**: θ ← θ − α ∇J (or an improved optimizer).

body.note: Why δ^{[L]} = a − y: for sigmoid with binary cross-entropy, ∂J/∂z = (∂J/∂a)(∂a/∂z) = (−y/a + (1 − y)/(1 − a)) · a(1 − a) = a − y. The same holds for softmax with cross-entropy and, trivially, for identity with squared error. It is the GLM property from the Generalized Linear Models chapter.

sections.title: A complete numerical example
body: Return to the network of the previous chapter: x = (1, 2), a hidden layer of two ReLU units with W^{[1]} = [[0.5, −1], [1, 0.5]] and b^{[1]} = (0, 0.5), and a sigmoid output with W^{[2]} = [1, −0.5] and b^{[2]} = 0.2. The label is y = 1.

example.title: Gradients of the loss by backpropagation
example.problem: Compute all the gradients of the cross-entropy loss, then take one gradient step with α = 0.5 and show that the loss falls.
solution: The first hidden unit was inactive (z = −1.5 < 0), so its gradient is exactly zero: ReLU blocks the error signal.

check.q: In the example, the first hidden unit receives zero gradient because
check.a: its pre-activation was negative, so ReLU′ = 0
wrong: the loss did not depend on it

sections.title: Vanishing and exploding gradients
body: Unrolling the recursion, the gradient reaching layer 1 is a product of one matrix and one diagonal derivative per layer:
A product of many factors tends to shrink toward zero or grow without bound, exponentially in the number of layers.

list: **Vanishing gradients.** The derivative of the sigmoid is at most 1/4. If each layer contributes a factor of about 0.25, the gradient through 10 layers is multiplied by 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶. The early layers receive almost no signal and learn extremely slowly. Saturated units (|z| large) have g′ ≈ 0 and block learning entirely.
**Exploding gradients.** If the weight matrices have norms above 1, the product grows exponentially and the updates become huge and unstable. This is common in recurrent networks.
**Dead ReLUs.** A ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for all inputs has zero gradient and never recovers.
**ReLU-family activations** have derivative 1 on the active side, so they do not shrink the signal.
**Careful initialization** keeps activations and gradients at a stable scale from the start (see Training Deep Networks).
**Normalization layers** (batch or layer normalization) re-center and re-scale the activations.
**Residual connections** let the gradient bypass layers: a block computes x + F(x), whose derivative is I + ∂F/∂x, never vanishing.
**Gradient clipping** rescales a gradient whose norm exceeds a threshold, which tames exploding gradients.
**Gated architectures** such as the LSTM were designed to carry information over long chains (see Sequence Models).

check.q: Why do deep sigmoid networks suffer from vanishing gradients?
check.a: The sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25, so the backward product shrinks exponentially with depth
wrong: Sigmoid networks have too many parameters

sections.title: Gradient checking and common bugs
body: Backpropagation code is easy to get subtly wrong and still produce a network that trains badly. **Gradient checking** compares the analytic gradient with a numerical estimate. For each parameter θ_j, use the central difference

and measure the relative difference ‖g_analytic − g_numeric‖ / (‖g_analytic‖ + ‖g_numeric‖). A value below about 10⁻⁷ is good; values around 10⁻³ or above signal a bug. The central difference has error O(ε²), far better than the one-sided O(ε).

list: Check on a tiny network and a few examples; each check needs two forward passes per parameter, so it is far too slow for training.
Turn off dropout and any randomness while checking.
Use double precision. In single precision the rounding error in J swamps the difference.
Beware ReLU kinks: if θ + ε crosses a kink the numerical gradient is wrong even when the code is right.

example.title: Checking one derivative
example.problem: For J(θ) = θ³ at θ = 2, compare the analytic derivative with the central difference using ε = 0.01.

body: Other classic bugs: forgetting to average over the batch, mixing up the transposes, applying the activation derivative at the wrong layer, using a stale (not recomputed) forward value, and being unable to overfit a tiny data set. A network should reach near-zero loss on 10 examples; if it cannot, something is broken.

check.q: Why is gradient checking done only for debugging?
check.a: It needs two forward passes per parameter, which is far too slow for real training
wrong: It is less accurate than backpropagation for large networks

summary: A computational graph breaks a computation into simple operations. Reverse-mode differentiation sends gradients backward, multiplying the upstream gradient by each local gradient.
Backpropagation computes all the gradients for about the cost of one forward pass, but it must store the forward activations.
Products of many Jacobians vanish or explode with depth. Use ReLU-type activations, good initialization, normalization, residual connections and gradient clipping.
Verify implementations with a central-difference gradient check, and make sure a tiny data set can be overfit.

problems.q: For f = (a·b + c)·d with a = 2, b = 3, c = −1, d = 4, compute f and all four partial derivatives by a forward and a backward pass.
problems.solution: Forward: u = ab = 6, v = u + c = 5, f = vd = 20. Backward: ∂f/∂v = d = 4 and ∂f/∂d = v = 5. v = u + c passes the gradient through: ∂f/∂u = 4 and ∂f/∂c = 4. u = ab gives ∂f/∂a = 4 · b = 12 and ∂f/∂b = 4 · a = 8.

problems.q: A logistic unit has z = 0.5, p = σ(z) = 0.622 and label y = 0. Find δ = ∂J/∂z for cross-entropy, and the gradient with respect to a weight whose input is 3.
problems.solution: δ = p − y = 0.622. The weight gradient is δ × input = 0.622 × 3 = 1.866.

problems.q: A 20-layer network has sigmoid units, and at each layer the backward factor is about 0.2. By what factor is the gradient at layer 1 reduced relative to the output layer?
problems.solution: There are 19 backward steps between the output and layer 1. 0.2¹⁰ = 1.02 × 10⁻⁷ and 0.2⁹ = 5.12 × 10⁻⁷, so 0.2¹⁹ = 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁴.
problems.a: About 5 × 10⁻¹⁴; there is essentially no gradient signal.

problems.q: Check by central difference with ε = 0.1 the derivative of J(θ) = θ² at θ = 3.
problems.solution: (3.1² − 2.9²)/0.2 = (9.61 − 8.41)/0.2 = 6.0, matching 2θ = 6 exactly (the central difference is exact for quadratics).

problems.q: A residual block computes y = x + F(x). If ∂F/∂x has all singular values below 0.1, what can you say about the gradient passing through the block?
problems.solution: The Jacobian is I + ∂F/∂x. Its singular values lie between 1 − 0.1 and 1 + 0.1, so the gradient is scaled by a factor between 0.9 and 1.1 and neither vanishes nor explodes quickly.
problems.a: The block scales the gradient by 0.9 to 1.1; the identity path preserves the signal.
